title: Refactor crypto adapter surface to enable OpenSSL 3.2 and lighter JWT path
creator: Priya Kapoor
description: Background: We have accumulated several ad-hoc crypto shims and multiple verification paths for tokens and SAML assertions across the runtime. This causes maintenance burden, increases binary size, and makes it difficult to provide a single FIPS/OpenSSL-compatible build. Goal: Consolidate the runtime crypto adapter surface into a small, well-tested abstraction that can be switched between legacy code and an OpenSSL 3.2 provider-backed implementation. Reduce hot-path allocations in token verification (JWT/JWE/JWS) and remove duplicated XML crypto code where we can rely on a compact, audited SAML verifier. Scope: - Introduce a single crypto facade (runtime/crypto/facade) with explicit, documented operations used by the serving runtime (sign/verify, hkdf/hmac, RSA/ECDSA verify, key import/derive). - Implement provider-backed OpenSSL 3.2 path that uses provider APIs and avoids deprecated public APIs. - Replace two in-house JWT verification paths with one JOSE facade layer using a small, battle-tested library (strip to only verifier code) and fallback to legacy when feature-flagged. - Replace legacy xmlsec-based SAML verification in the non-enterprise path with a minimal SAML verifier implemented as a narrow parser+signature-check stage; keep xmlsec for enterprise builds behind a build flag. - Reduce allocations and locking in token hot-path: pre-allocated stacks for common key sizes, reuse EVP_PKEY objects in pooled fashion, and remove intermediate byte-array copies in verification route. Success criteria: - OpenSSL 3.2 provider path builds in CI and passes all unit/integration tests. - p50 token-verify latency reduced by >= 10% in our synthetic token workload. - Binary size for the inference runtime decreases or remains within 3% of current release for non-enterprise builds. - No increase in token verification error rate in canary traffic. Out of scope: - Any major protocol changes to OAuth flows or customer-facing token formats. - Full removal of xmlsec enterprise path in this sprint; we will gate that behind an enterprise-flag roadmap item. Rollout plan: 1) Implement facade and provider-backed OpenSSL branch behind build tag (openss_provider). 2) Add CI matrix job that runs unit tests with OpenSSL 1.1.1, OpenSSL 3.0, and OpenSSL 3.2. 3) Add runtime feature flag to select new crypto facade at process startup. 4) Canary the new provider on 1% traffic for dedicated customers with token-heavy routes; monitor token-parse-errors and SSL handshake metrics. 5) Gradually increase to 10% and then 50% contingent on metrics. Risks & mitigations: - Risk: behavior differences between OpenSSL versions cause signature verification divergence. Mitigation: add cross-version verification tests and sign a set of golden tokens with each verifier to compare results. - Risk: subtle buffer reuse introduces safety bugs. Mitigation: preserve a debug build that enables ASAN/UBSAN and run fuzz targets for JWT/JWE parsing. - Risk: enterprise customers that rely on xmlsec semantics may be affected. Mitigation: keep enterprise build path unchanged and coordinate with account owners before changing defaults. Links & artifacts: - Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/ENG/Crypto+Facade+-+Design - PR (initial facade + tests): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3412 - Benchmark notes: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1a2b3c-token-verify-bench - CI matrix draft: https://github.com/redwood-inference/actions/runs/562233
